title: A Classroom Management Plan That Works
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Opening with an anecdote about creative figures who worked with the simplest of materials, Linsin argues that an effective classroom management plan needs no elaborate design—just consistent enforcement. He frames the plan as a contract that binds the teacher to protect students' right to learn and enjoy school, with exactly two purposes: stating the rules and stating what happens when rules are broken. He explicitly rejects incorporating rewards or incentive systems, calling the 'do this and get that' mentality a short-term fix that doesn't change behavior long-term. His recommended plan includes four rules (listen and follow directions, raise your hand, keep hands and feet to yourself, respect classmates and teacher) paired with an escalating three-step consequence sequence: warning, time-out, letter home. Linsin closes by warning against decorative, 'cutesy' presentation, recommending a plain, serious poster-board display that reflects the plan's narrow but high-priority purpose, and reminding teachers that the plan only works if honored exactly as written.
points: An effective classroom management plan needs no elaborate design—just two purposes: stating rules and stating consequences.
Reject reward and incentive systems as a short-term fix that doesn't actually change student behavior long-term.
The recommended plan uses four core rules and an escalating three-step consequence sequence: warning, time-out, letter home.
The plan's usefulness comes entirely from how consistently it's implemented and enforced, not from the plan itself.
Present the plan plainly and seriously—large poster board with rules and consequences—rather than with cutesy or colorful designs.
quotes: His point is that there is zero correlation between creative talent and the materials and equipment used.
There is no magic in the plan itself. It has no power to influence behavior. Only you have the power to influence behavior by creating a classroom your students want to be part of.
A classroom management plan is a contract you make with your students that promises you will protect their right to learn and enjoy school without interference.
The “do this and get that” mentality is a short-term solution that may get you through the day, and thus is a good strategy for substitute teachers, but it won’t actually change behavior.
Its usefulness comes from how it’s implemented, enforced, and carried out, from how you communicate with your students, from how much leverage you have with them.
Avoid cutesy and colorful designs. Even kindergarteners need to know that your classroom management plan and the rules by which it governs are sacred, serious.
